This ability, known as bioluminescence, results from a chemical reaction in which an enzyme causes a light-emitting molecule to release energy as a soft blue or green glow. Blue light travels further through seawater than any other colour, which explains why so few deep-sea animals glow red. The uses to which this light is put are remarkably varied. Some fish dangle a glowing lure in front of their mouths to attract unsuspecting prey, while certain squid illuminate their undersides so that their silhouette disappears against the faint light filtering down from above, making them almost invisible to predators below. Other species release clouds of luminous fluid to startle an attacker and escape under cover of the distraction. Scientists estimate that as many as three-quarters of the animals living in the deep sea are capable of producing light, yet the phenomenon remained poorly understood until relatively recently. questions.passage: Predicting exactly when a volcano will erupt remains one of the great challenges of earth science, but the task is no longer the guesswork it once was. Before an eruption, molten rock usually rises towards the surface, and as it does so it leaves a series of tell-tale signs. Swarms of small earthquakes often increase in frequency as the rock forces its way through cracks in the crust. The ground above may swell by a few centimetres, a change that can now be detected by satellites orbiting hundreds of kilometres overhead. Scientists also monitor the gases escaping from vents, since a sudden rise in sulphur dioxide can indicate that fresh magma is approaching. None of these signals, however, guarantees that an eruption is imminent. Magma sometimes rises, stalls and cools without ever breaking through, and a volcano may show signs of unrest for years before settling down again. This uncertainty places authorities in a difficult position. Ordering an evacuation too early can cause economic hardship and erode public trust if nothing happens, whereas waiting too long can cost lives. For this reason, volcanologists increasingly express their forecasts as probabilities rather than firm predictions.

This soft-bodied relative of the snail can open screw-top jars, find its way through mazes and recognise individual human beings, reportedly squirting water at keepers it dislikes. What makes these achievements so intriguing is that the octopus's nervous system is organised quite differently from ours. Roughly two-thirds of its neurons are located not in its brain but in its eight arms, each of which appears able to taste, touch and even make simple decisions independently. An arm that has been separated from the body will, for a short time, continue to reach for food. Researchers believe that this arrangement evolved to coordinate limbs that have no bones and can bend in any direction, a control problem far too complex for a single central brain to manage alone. questions.passage: Anyone who has watched a thunderstorm will have noticed that lightning is followed, sooner or later, by thunder. The delay arises because light travels almost a million times faster than sound, so counting the seconds between flash and rumble gives a rough idea of how far away the storm is: about three seconds for every kilometre. Yet the mechanism that produces lightning in the first place is still not fully understood. Inside a storm cloud, tiny ice crystals and heavier pellets of soft hail collide as they are carried up and down by powerful air currents. These collisions transfer electric charge, so that the top of the cloud becomes positively charged and the lower part negative. When the difference grows large enough, the air can no longer act as an insulator and a giant spark bridges the gap. What puzzles physicists is that the electric fields measured inside clouds seem too weak to trigger a discharge on their own. One theory holds that particles arriving from outer space knock electrons loose and start a chain reaction, but this has yet to be confirmed. Thunder itself is easier to explain: the lightning heats the surrounding air so rapidly that it expands explosively.

The obvious solution, farming spiders as we farm silkworms, has proved impractical: spiders are solitary, territorial and inclined to eat one another when kept together. Researchers have therefore turned to genetic engineering, inserting spider silk genes into bacteria, yeast and even goats, whose milk can then be processed to extract silk proteins. Producing the proteins turned out to be the easier part of the problem. Spinning them into a fibre with the properties of natural silk is far harder, because the spider's own spinning gland subjects the liquid protein to a precise sequence of changes in acidity, pressure and stretching that is extremely difficult to reproduce. Early artificial fibres were consequently weaker than the real thing. Recent attempts have come closer, and companies now sell small quantities of bio-engineered silk for products such as sports clothing. Applications under consideration range from surgical stitches to lightweight body armour.

Modern seismologists are generally cautious to the point of refusing to make predictions at all, at least in the sense of naming a time, a place and a magnitude in advance. What they can do is produce long-term forecasts. By studying the history of a fault and measuring how fast the rocks on either side are moving, they can estimate the likelihood of a large earthquake in a region over the coming decades. Such forecasts are invaluable for drawing up building codes and deciding where hospitals and schools should be located. A more recent development is early warning. Because the most damaging seismic waves travel more slowly than the first, weaker ones, sensors near the epicentre can detect a quake and send an alert to more distant cities before the strong shaking arrives. The warning may last only a few seconds, but that is enough to stop trains, halt surgery or allow people to take cover.

The moon's gravity pulls on the oceans, drawing water towards the side of the Earth that faces it. Less intuitively, a second bulge of water forms on the opposite side of the planet, where the moon's pull is weakest. As the Earth rotates through these two bulges, most coasts experience two high tides and two low tides roughly every day. When the sun and moon line up, at new moon and full moon, their combined pull produces especially large tides, known as spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. When they are at right angles to each other, the tides are weaker. Local geography, however, can override these general patterns dramatically. In some funnel-shaped bays, the difference between high and low water exceeds fifteen metres, while parts of the Mediterranean see barely any tide at all. The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like pieces of a jigsaw puzzle, identical fossils of land animals had been found on continents separated by vast oceans, and rock formations seemed to continue from one side of the Atlantic to the other. What Wegener could not provide was a convincing mechanism. He suggested that the continents ploughed through the ocean floor, but physicists calculated that the forces involved would be nowhere near strong enough. Many geologists preferred to believe that land bridges, since sunk beneath the sea, had once allowed animals to cross between continents. Wegener died in 1930 on an expedition to Greenland, his theory still rejected. Vindication came only in the 1960s, when surveys of the ocean floor revealed that new crust is constantly being created along underwater mountain ranges and pushing older crust outwards. The resulting theory of plate tectonics showed that Wegener had been right about the movement, though wrong about how it happened.

Within a fraction of a second, it can change not only the colour of its skin but also its pattern and even its texture, raising small bumps to imitate rock or seaweed. This is made possible by millions of tiny pigment sacs in the skin, each surrounded by muscles controlled directly by the nervous system, which allows far faster changes than the hormone-driven colour shifts of a chameleon. What has long puzzled biologists is that the cuttlefish appears to be colour-blind, possessing only one type of light receptor in its eyes. How, then, does it match its surroundings so accurately? Some researchers believe that the unusual U-shaped pupil allows the animal to detect colour indirectly, by exploiting the way different wavelengths come into focus at slightly different distances. Others have found light-sensitive proteins in the skin itself, raising the intriguing possibility that the cuttlefish can, in some sense, see with its body. The question has not been resolved, but it illustrates how much remains to be learned about animal senses.

questions.passage: Long before air conditioning was invented, people living in some of the hottest regions on earth found ingenious ways of keeping their homes cool. Traditional houses in parts of the Middle East and North Africa, for instance, were often built around shaded courtyards, with thick walls of mud brick or stone that absorbed heat during the day and released it slowly at night. Some featured tall towers known as wind catchers, which captured breezes above the rooftops and directed them down into the rooms below, sometimes passing the air over water to cool it further. Narrow streets kept buildings in each other's shade, and small windows limited the entry of sunlight. Such designs, developed over centuries through trial and error rather than scientific calculation, are often described as vernacular architecture. For much of the twentieth century, they were dismissed as old-fashioned and replaced by glass-fronted buildings that depend entirely on mechanical cooling. As energy costs rise and temperatures climb, however, architects are increasingly studying traditional techniques to see what can be learned from them. The aim is not to reproduce old buildings exactly but to adapt their underlying principles, combining them with modern materials and technologies to create buildings that require far less energy to remain comfortable.

questions.passage: Place names are among the most durable elements of any language. Cities may be rebuilt, populations replaced and languages abandoned, yet the names of rivers, hills and settlements often survive, preserving traces of peoples who have otherwise vanished from the historical record. The study of place names can therefore offer valuable evidence to historians. In many parts of Europe, for example, the names of major rivers are older than any language currently spoken in the region, and their original meanings can only be guessed at. Names of villages frequently reveal how a landscape was once used, referring to features such as clearings in a forest, fords across a river or the crops that were grown nearby. They may also record the arrival of new groups, since settlers often named places in their own language, leaving distinctive layers that can be mapped. Interpreting this evidence, however, requires caution. Over centuries, names are worn down and reshaped by speakers who no longer understand them, and they may come to resemble unrelated words. Popular explanations of a name's origin are frequently based on such misleading resemblances, and local legends have sometimes been invented specifically to explain a name whose real meaning had long been forgotten.

Powerful lenses developed in the nineteenth century allowed a relatively small flame to be seen from many kilometres away, and the introduction of electricity reduced the need for constant attention. By the late twentieth century, most lighthouses had been fully automated and the last keepers withdrawn. Today satellite navigation means that ships rely far less on lights than they once did. People with perfect pitch almost always began musical training at a very early age, usually before the age of six, which suggests that there may be a critical period during which the ability can develop. It also appears to be considerably more common among speakers of tone languages, in which the pitch of a word can change its meaning, presumably because these speakers are trained from infancy to pay close attention to pitch. Interestingly, perfect pitch is not necessarily an advantage. Musicians who have it may find it uncomfortable to perform with instruments tuned slightly differently from the standard, and some report difficulty recognising a familiar melody when it is played in an unfamiliar key. Most professional musicians manage perfectly well without it, relying instead on relative pitch, the ability to judge the distance between notes, which can be improved through training at any age.

Satisfying necessary desires is easy and brings lasting contentment, he argued, whereas pursuing empty ones leads only to anxiety, since there is always more to want. The highest pleasure, in his view, was a calm state of mind free from pain and fear. To achieve it, he recommended a simple diet, the company of good friends and the study of philosophy, which he believed could free people from irrational fears, above all the fear of death. Monasteries had been among the first institutions to require precise timekeeping, since monks were obliged to gather for prayer at fixed points throughout the day and night. The spread of public clocks gradually changed how ordinary people experienced time. Towns competed to install the most impressive clocks, which became symbols of civic pride as well as practical tools. Merchants and employers began to measure work by the hour rather than by the task or by daylight, and the idea of punctuality acquired new importance. The puzzles remain valuable less for their conclusions than for the questions about space, time and infinity that they force us to confront.

Later, as European sea voyages expanded, maps became valuable commercial and political tools, and some governments treated the most accurate charts as state secrets. Even the treatment of unknown territory changed over time. Earlier mapmakers had often filled gaps with speculation or decoration, but by the eighteenth century it became fashionable to leave unexplored areas blank, a choice that signalled scientific honesty. Yet those blank spaces were rarely empty in reality; they were inhabited by peoples whose own knowledge of the land was simply ignored. In this sense, a blank space could imply that a region was available for exploration and conquest. Additional names were therefore added, and they tended to fall into a few broad categories. Some described a person's occupation, such as baker or smith; others referred to a place, such as a hill, a river or the name of a village; others identified a father; and still others were nicknames based on appearance or character. At first, these names were not fixed and might change from one generation to the next, but over the centuries they gradually became hereditary. Surnames can therefore preserve information about the lives of distant ancestors, although caution is needed. Spellings changed, names were sometimes recorded incorrectly by officials, and families occasionally adopted new names altogether. In some cultures, moreover, hereditary surnames were introduced only in the nineteenth or twentieth centuries, often as a result of government reforms.

Fluctuations in temperature and humidity can cause materials to expand and contract, leading to cracks in paintings and furniture, while insects and pollution pose additional threats. Balancing preservation with access is a constant challenge. A museum's purpose is to allow people to see its collections, yet every hour of display shortens an object's life. Contracts, leases and terms of service are often written in long, convoluted sentences crammed with archaic expressions, double negatives and cross-references, so that ordinary readers sign them without understanding what they have agreed to. Lawyers have traditionally defended this style on the grounds of precision: familiar formulas, they argue, have been interpreted by courts over many years, and departing from them risks introducing uncertainty. The plain-language movement rejects this reasoning. Its supporters maintain that clarity and precision are not opposites, and that a document written in short sentences with everyday vocabulary can be every bit as exact as one written in traditional legalese. Several governments now require consumer contracts and official forms to be written in plain language, and some studies have found that clearer documents reduce the number of disputes and enquiries, saving money for organisations as well as their customers. Resistance persists nonetheless. Some lawyers suspect that simplifying documents may make their expertise appear less necessary, while others simply find it difficult to abandon habits acquired during years of training.

Many people remain unaware that the option exists, or find the prospect of standing before a judge intimidating, however relaxed the proceedings are meant to be. Businesses, which may appear in such courts regularly, can gain an advantage simply through familiarity with the process. Even winning a case does not always mean being paid, since the court's decision must sometimes be enforced through further steps. Politicians who wish to appear tough on crime have often been reluctant to promote them, fearing that the public will see them as a soft option. The evidence, however, tends to favour them. Short prison terms frequently disrupt the very things that help people stay out of trouble, such as stable housing, employment and family relationships, while exposing first-time offenders to more experienced criminals. Studies in several countries have found that people given community sentences are less likely to reoffend than comparable offenders sent to prison for a few months. Community punishment is also considerably cheaper. In several cases, the change reflects the worldview of indigenous communities who have long regarded the river or mountain as an ancestor rather than a resource. Supporters argue that the approach offers stronger protection than conventional environmental regulation, since it allows cases to be brought on behalf of the ecosystem itself, rather than only by people who can prove that they personally have suffered harm. Without such data, they argue, failing schools could escape scrutiny for years. Critics, however, point to a range of unintended consequences. When test scores determine a school's reputation or its teachers' pay, there is a powerful incentive to 'teach to the test', concentrating on the narrow skills that are measured at the expense of subjects such as art, music and history. Pupils may learn to recognise question types rather than to understand ideas deeply. High stakes can also produce considerable anxiety among children and, in extreme cases, outright cheating by adults. Some countries offer every citizen a personal learning account, a sum of money that can be spent on approved courses at any stage of their career. Online courses have made it possible to study at home in the evening, fitting learning around work and family. Yet participation remains strikingly unequal. But small reductions, for instance from twenty-eight pupils to twenty-five, tend to make little measurable difference, perhaps because teachers continue to teach in much the same way regardless of the number in front of them. Reducing class sizes is also extremely expensive, since it requires both additional teachers and additional classrooms. Because they are scattered through residential streets, pocket parks bring greenery within a few minutes' walk of people who would otherwise have no access to nature, including elderly residents unable to travel far. Trees and plants help to cool the surrounding streets in summer and absorb rainwater that would otherwise overwhelm drains. Such spaces can also become informal meeting points, where neighbours who might never otherwise speak strike up conversations. Their success depends heavily on maintenance, however. Shop owners tend to overestimate how many of their customers arrive by car, and people who cycle or walk to the shops, although they spend less per visit, return more frequently and often spend more over the course of a month. As for congestion, the effect is less straightforward than it might appear. In the short term, reallocating road space can slow traffic, but over time some drivers change their routes, their times of travel or their mode of transport altogether. Planners call this phenomenon 'traffic evaporation', the mirror image of the well-known tendency for new roads to fill up with extra traffic. The quality of the lanes matters enormously. This clock cannot reset itself instantly; it typically adjusts by about an hour per day, so a traveller who crosses eight time zones may take more than a week to recover fully. Governing bodies have introduced protocols requiring players with suspected concussion to leave the field for assessment, and in some cases to rest for a set period before returning. Rules on tackling have been tightened, and some youth leagues have restricted heading the ball in football training. These measures have not satisfied everyone.
